opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it's because their world is so concrete. When I go to teach, the kids are thinking about whether they'll finish their homework before dinner, whether their parents will call this week from the city where they work, whether they can get a turn on the one shared phone to watch a cartoon. If I walk in and start talking about large language models, scaling laws, or which company just released which model, it just floats right over their heads. It doesn't connect to anything they live with.

And I think there's something a bit uncomfortable about it, too. In my daily work, AI feels like the center of the universe. Everyone around me is talking about AGI, about how everything is going to change in a few years. Then I spend a weekend with these children, and I realize that for a huge part of the world, none of that conversation has arrived yet. The gap isn't only in knowledge. It's in what feels urgent. For them, what matters is having an adult who shows up consistently, who listens, who notices when they're upset.

So I made a choice not to bring my "work self" into that classroom. I teach them reading, a little math, sometimes we just draw or play games. If a kid asks me what I do, I'll say something simple, like "I help teach computers to understand language." Sometimes they think that's really cool, sometimes they don't care at all. Both are fine.

But it has also made me reflect. If this technology really is going to reshape society, then these kids are the ones who will live in that future the longest. And right now they have almost no voice in how it's being built. So even though I don't talk about AI with them, being with them keeps reminding me who I'm supposed to be building it for.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the children may have to wait for a turn on their one shared phone, then explains that AI talk does not connect to their lives.

fable-5.1.text:
Because when I'm standing in that classroom, the gap between what I do in my day job and what's in front of me is enormous. I spend my week thinking about model capabilities, agents, how fast all of this is moving. Then I take the bus out to the village school, and the kids I'm teaching are maybe ten, eleven years old. Some of them share one old smartphone with their grandparents. The school has a computer room, but half the machines don't turn on, and the internet drops whenever it rains.

So if I walked in and said, "Let's talk about large language models," it would feel almost like a performance. For whom? Not for them. They don't lack information about AI. They lack the things underneath it: confidence that their questions are worth asking, someone who shows up every week, a reason to believe the world outside the county is a place they're allowed to enter.

I'll give you a concrete example. I once tried to show a few of them a chatbot on my phone, thinking it would be fun. They were polite, a little curious, and then one girl asked me whether it could help her write a letter to her mother who works in Shenzhen. That stopped me. The technology wasn't the point. What she actually needed was a way to say something to her mother. I could have taught her that with a pencil.

So that's what I mean by "too far removed." It's not that these kids can't understand AI. They could, easily. It's that if I lead with it, I'm answering a question nobody in that room is asking. My job there is to listen first and figure out what they're actually asking. Most of the time, it's much more basic and much more human. And honestly, that's been good for me too. It reminds me what all this technology is supposed to be for.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes the children sharing one old smartphone, broken school computers, and unreliable internet, then connects that situation to why leading a lesson with AI would feel remote from them.

astra-6.text: I think it’s because their everyday concerns are much more immediate—understanding a lesson, finishing their homework, figuring out what they’re good at. If I start talking about how AI will change the world, that can feel very abstract. It’s not that they can’t understand it; I need to give them a reason to care and connect it to something they already know. Otherwise, I’m just talking about what interests me instead of paying attention to what they need.

r001.rationale: The response says AI may feel abstract compared with the children’s immediate concerns, but does not link this to their lack of access to electronic devices.

sol-6.1.text: Because for the children I volunteer to teach, AI can feel quite abstract. Their more immediate concerns are understanding their lessons and figuring out what opportunities they might have. If I start with a big discussion about AI, it may have little connection to their everyday lives. I’d rather begin with something familiar and help them see where technology might actually be useful to them.

r001.rationale: The response says AI may feel abstract and disconnected from the children’s everyday concerns, but it does not link that distance to their lack of access to electronic devices.
